prompt: What three things does a certificate bind together?
hint: Look at the first two captures.

choices.text: A name, a key and a signature
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A name, a private key and a password
choices.why: A certificate never holds a private key.

choices.text: A domain, an IP address and a session key
choices.why: No session key is in a certificate.

choices.text: The server's hostname, its operating system and its owner's tax id
choices.why: Those are not in a TLS certificate.

prompt: Anybody can download Vereda's portal certificate. Why can't an impostor simply serve that copy?

choices.text: Browsers detect copied certificates by their serial number
choices.why: The serial is public too.

choices.text: The certificate is encrypted to the real server
choices.why: Certificates are public and unencrypted.

choices.text: Only the real server holds the private key
choices.why: Right: holding the private key is what is proved.

choices.text: The CA is contacted on every connection
choices.why: No CA takes part in each connection.

prompt: What does a domain-validated (DV) certificate for `portal.vereda.example` assert?

choices.text: That Vereda is a licensed clinic
choices.why: No check on the business was made.

choices.text: That the site is free of malware
choices.why: CAs check control of names, not content.

choices.text: Whoever requested it controlled that domain
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: That the portal's code was audited
choices.why: Not a CA's job.

prompt: Why is a root certificate's issuer the same as its subject?

choices.text: Because the lab built it carelessly
choices.why: Every root looks like this.

choices.text: It is self-signed: nobody is above it
choices.why: Right: its trust comes from the trust store.

choices.text: Because roots are signed by the browser
choices.why: Browsers sign nothing; they hold lists.

choices.text: So that it can be revoked by itself
choices.why: That is not the reason, and revoking a root is not how removal works.

prompt: Match each certificate to its basic constraints.
Why does Vereda keep its root offline and sign servers with an issuing CA instead?

choices.text: Because a root key cannot sign server certificates
choices.why: It technically can; it should not.

choices.text: Because issuing CAs use stronger algorithms
choices.why: Strength is not the reason.

choices.text: A leaked issuing CA is replaced in an afternoon; a root takes years
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: To make the chain longer and harder to forge
choices.why: Length adds no strength.

prompt: In `openssl verify -show_chain`, at what depth is the root?
Verified against the system's trust store, the portal's chain fails. What is the right fix on Vereda's staff laptops?

choices.text: Turn verification off for internal hosts
choices.why: That accepts anybody who answers.

choices.text: Install Vereda's root on them
choices.why: Right: by configuration management or device policy.

choices.text: Buy a public certificate for the root
choices.why: A root is not something a public CA sells.

choices.text: Add the portal certificate to the browser's exceptions
choices.why: An exception per site is the same as not checking.

prompt: A server works in Chrome on one laptop but `curl` reports `unable to get local issuer certificate`. Most likely cause?
hint: Some browsers fetch what is missing.

choices.text: curl does not support elliptic-curve certificates
choices.why: It does.

choices.text: The certificate has expired
choices.why: That error would say expired.

choices.text: The server does not send the intermediate
choices.why: Right: serve the full chain.

choices.text: Chrome is less secure than curl
choices.why: Both check; Chrome papered over the gap.

prompt: The impostor root has exactly Vereda's root's name. Why did the forged portal certificate fail against the real root?

choices.text: The impostor's certificate had expired
choices.why: It is valid until 2041.

choices.text: Signatures are checked against keys
choices.why: Right: the fingerprints differ.

choices.text: The names differed in an invisible character
choices.why: They are identical.

choices.text: OpenSSL keeps a list of impostors
choices.why: No such list exists.

prompt: How many root certificates did the recording machine's Mozilla bundle hold?
hint: The first command of the section.

prompt: What does Certificate Transparency give a domain owner?

choices.text: A guarantee that no CA can issue for the domain
choices.why: CAs still can; they cannot do it unseen.

choices.text: Visibility of every certificate any public CA issued for it
choices.why: Right: and to be alerted to one nobody requested.

choices.text: Encryption of the certificate's contents
choices.why: Certificates stay public.

choices.text: Free certificates
choices.why: That is Let's Encrypt, a CA.

prompt: What does a CAA record `0 issue "letsencrypt.org"` on `vereda.example` do?

choices.text: Tells other CAs to refuse to issue for the domain
choices.why: Right: it stops honest CAs from being tricked.

choices.text: Forces browsers to accept only Let's Encrypt for the domain
choices.why: Browsers do not read CAA.

choices.text: Revokes certificates from other CAs
choices.why: CAA does not revoke anything.

choices.text: Encrypts DNS answers for the domain
choices.why: That is not what it does.

prompt: What is the maximum lifetime of a public TLS certificate from March 2027, in days?
Order the certificates of Vereda's chain from the one a client trusts first to the one it checks last.
Which of these would let somebody impersonate `portal.vereda.example` to Vereda's staff laptops? Choose all that apply.
hint: Whoever can make a chain end in a trusted root.

choices.text: Installing their own root on the laptops
choices.why: Yes: the impostor root verified in the lab.

choices.text: Stealing the issuing CA's private key
choices.why: Yes: they could sign any name.

choices.text: Downloading the portal's public certificate
choices.why: Without its private key it proves nothing.

choices.text: Creating a root with the same name as Vereda's
choices.why: The name alone fails against the real key.

pairs.right: an honest CA tricked into issuing

right_distractors: a weak password on the portal
